extra.title: Three changes in five years
extra.surface:
The Resource Guide asks each participant one question: if the United States could make only three major changes in the next five years to accelerate discovery and commercialization, what should they be? Here are mine.

Access

A supported front door, with a named person responsible for the first handoff, for people and groups with no institution behind them.

Capacity

Fund the engineering, maintenance, and independent validation that make a discovery usable, as translation work in its own right.

Learning

Shared, interoperable records of what was tried, what happened, why it stopped, and what should happen next.
extra.mid:
ChangeBarrier it removes (Guide question 1)Intervention (Guide question 2)Journey stage (Guide question 3)
AccessEligibility without a usable path in; no introductions, no grants staffNavigation and referral pilot with accountable handoffDiscovery to Translation
CapacityPrototype cannot become something others rely on; maintenance unfundedTechnical assistance network; stewardship funded as translationTranslation to Validation to Scale
LearningResults reduced to pass/fail; failures lost; repeated reviewFederated research records with a small common schemaValidation, and evaluating repeated support
extra.deep:
The Guide frames the convening as a move from observation to barrier, root cause, intervention, and action. Each of the three changes is written that way on this site: the barrier is stated at the surface, the root cause and the intervention at mid-level, and the evidence and open questions in the deep dive.

They also answer the Guide's question 7, access to innovation: who has access to the ecosystem and who does not. Independent contributors, small nonprofits, and community organizations are the people these changes are for.

extra.deep:
Seven breakout points, answered once for the whole position:

PointAnswer
1. ChallengeCapable independent contributors and community organizations cannot convert eligibility into entry, and prototypes cannot become maintained, validated tools.
2. Root causeSupport systems assume an institution: staff, offices, infrastructure, introductions. Maintenance and validation are unfunded and invisible.
3. Existing modelsSBIR/STTR, I-Corps, TIP Translation to Practice, OSF and Registered Reports, open-source foundations.
4. GapsNo accountable first handoff; no stewardship funding; no interoperable record of what happened and why.
5. RecommendationsAccess pilot, capacity network, learning records: three bounded pilots.
6. StakeholdersNSF TIP and SBIR/STTR, EPSCoR institutions, university CTSIs, open-source foundations, community nonprofits, NIST tech transfer.
7. MeasuresCompleted connections, progress toward validation, sustained reuse, resolved uncertainty. Not visits or award counts.

extra.title: What the SBIR readings mean for people like me
extra.surface: The participant handout's four SBIR readings disagree about how hard to push commercialization, but they agree on one thing: judge awards by what they produced, not by how many there were. That is the same argument as my learning priority.
extra.mid:
• Cohen, Feldman and Stern: SBIR is mission infrastructure; success looks different across agencies; use many measures and better integrated data.
  • Schönander: reauthorization is not enough; open the door to first-time applicants; assess commercialization readiness explicitly; try lotteries and golden tickets for ideas consensus review misses.
  • Katz: seed funding should graduate firms; weight commercial viability heavily; provide procurement pathways.
  • Murphy (SBA): ask what past awards produced; share past-performance and technical learning across agencies.

Common thread: reward demonstrable progress and learning. That needs records richer than pass or fail.
extra.deep:
Where an independent contributor sits in that debate:

Reading's concernWhat this position adds
New entrants are discouragedA navigation service with an accountable handoff lowers the first step for individuals and informal teams.
Commercialization readiness should be assessed with evidenceCriterion-level records (parity, accuracy, performance, production readiness kept separate) are that evidence for technical products.
Past performance should capture learning, not award countsDispositions beyond pass/fail: blocked, inconclusive, failed-a-requirement, corrected. Publish them.
Fix the transition system, not only the awardTechnical assistance network for validation, packaging, deployment, and documentation.

Sources: Participant handout bibliography: Cohen, Feldman, Stern (2026) · Schönander (2026)

extra.title: Where the journey slows down
extra.surface: The Guide draws the path as Discovery, Translation, Validation, Commercialization, Scale, Impact. From where I stand, the slowdowns are at two joints: getting from Discovery into Translation without an institution, and getting from Translation through Validation without funded engineering.
extra.mid:
StageWhat slows it for independentsWhich change helps
Discovery to TranslationNo entry path, no introductionsAccess
Translation to ValidationNo funded engineering, no independent replication, no second hardwareCapacity
Validation to CommercializationEvidence not legible to funders or buyersLearning
Scale and ImpactMaintenance unfunded; dependencies rotCapacity
extra.deep: The Guide's AI question belongs here too. AI shortens Discovery and Translation. It does not shorten Validation unless verification capacity grows with it. The Dell'Acqua "jagged frontier" finding cited in the Guide matches what the Mojo record shows in miniature: capable on one task, unreliable on a similar one, so test per task and keep the gates fixed before the run.

commercial.title: From research kernels to a product: physics modeling on affordable GPUs
commercial.surface:
The same Mojo kernels that were checked for accuracy are the building blocks of a product idea: validated scientific computing that runs on affordable AMD graphics hardware, not only on the most expensive accelerators. Our exploratory warp-field physics model is the first workload.

Validated first, fast second. The accuracy record is the sales sheet.

proposed kernels documented
commercial.mid:
• What exists: six GPU kernel classes (Laplacian, diffusion, derivative stencil, RK4, atomics, STREAM Triad) ported to Mojo and run on an AMD gfx1103 integrated GPU, with HIP comparisons and a 24-case accuracy assessment. Repository: KosMojAMD.
  • Why it could sell: research groups and small companies often own AMD or mixed hardware. Portable kernels with a retained accuracy record lower the cost of trusting a result on the machine you already have.
  • Who would buy or fund it: computational-physics groups, engineering simulation shops, HPC centers wanting a second vendor, and SBIR/STTR-scale ventures that need validated building blocks rather than a full platform.
  • What it is not yet: not a benchmarked product, not a library with a support contract, not proof of speed. Float32 failed accuracy; Float64 passed. Speed was never qualified.

Roadmap ask. Treat validated kernel libraries as fundable translation work: small awards for qualification, packaging, documentation, and independent replication on second hardware.

Question for the room. Would an SBIR-scale award for a validated, vendor-portable numerical kernel library be a good use of translation funding? What would the reviewers need to see?
commercial.deep:
Product hypothesis, stated so it can be tested

ClaimStatusEvidence or gap
Mojo kernels run correctly on an AMD integrated GPU (gfx1103)documentedKosMojAMD evidence folders, HIP byte-parity 24/24, Float64 within frozen limits
Results are portable across vendorsin developmentOne AMD device tested; no NVIDIA or second AMD device in the retained record
Faster or cheaper than the incumbent pathproposedNo qualified benchmark; performance qualification explicitly not supplied by S02-I
A team would pay for a supported libraryproposedNo customer discovery yet; this convening is the first outside audience
Warp-field physics as the anchor workloaddocumentedComputational-Spacetime-Dynamics-Research campaign records; exploratory, motivating hypothesis unproven

Path to a first paid engagement

  1. Qualify two more kernels to the same protocol on the same device. Publish the ledger.
  2. Replicate on a second GPU, ideally a different vendor. Record differences honestly.
  3. Benchmark only the qualified kernels; report speed, memory, and accuracy together.
  4. Package as a small library with a versioned accuracy contract and a support offer.
  5. Pilot with one research group that owns AMD hardware and a stencil-heavy model.

The physics story stays honest: the warp-field model is a mathematical exploration that produced reusable tooling. The tooling, not the propulsion, is the product.

Sources: KosMojAMD · Assessment 2026-08-20 · Computational-Spacetime-Dynamics-Research

notes.message: Here is the whole talk in one breath. America can grow its innovation capacity by making it easier for three groups to get support, check their work, and put results into practice: independent researchers, open-source builders, and community organizations. Three priorities: access, capacity, learning. Everything else I say is an example of one of those three.
notes.pathway: I have done useful technical work with no institution behind me. Being eligible for a program is not the same as having a way in. There is no grants office, no tech-transfer desk, no one to make the introduction. My question for the room: who owns the first handoff when someone has promising work and no institution?
notes.portal: A portal helps only if someone is responsible for what happens after the match. Funding search already exists. What is missing is a named navigator, opportunity records that say when they were verified, and tracking of whether a referral actually connected. Measure connections, not visits.
notes.opensource: Research runs on software somebody has to test, document, secure, and maintain. That work is translation. Fund stewardship and adoption explicitly, and let the money reach independent maintainers, not only institutions.
notes.modernization: We rewrote part of our scientific tooling in Mojo and checked it against the established implementation. Across 24 cases both gave exactly the same answers. Then we compared against independent mathematical references. Float64 passed. Float32 failed. So two programs can agree perfectly and still miss the target. Agreement and accuracy are different questions. We kept the failure on the record. Nothing was rerun for this talk.
notes.commercial: Here is the commercial angle. Those same validated kernels are the seed of a product: scientific computing you can trust on affordable AMD graphics hardware, not only on the most expensive accelerators. Our warp-field model is the first workload. The pitch is validated first, fast second. What is missing is a second device, a benchmark, and a first customer. That is exactly the size of an SBIR-style award.
notes.gkos: When AI helps with research, someone later has to ask what evidence supports this, what is uncertain, and what the action was allowed to do. GKOS is my developing approach to keeping those links. Provenance lets you inspect a claim. It does not make the claim true.
notes.verification: AI makes producing artifacts cheap. Checking them is now the bottleneck. Confidence and fluent explanations are not acceptance criteria. Set gates before the run. Keep corrections visible. Budget verification alongside acceleration.
notes.library: Connect existing repositories through a shared catalog and a small common record. Owners keep their data. The record keeps what was tried, what happened, why, and what came next. Pilot it small.
notes.dispositions: One word cannot carry what an experiment taught us. The Mojo test passed one check and failed another in the same run. Blocked, aborted, inconclusive, outside domain, and failed-a-requirement are different things. And a missing record is not proof that nothing ran. Say unknown.
notes.storage: Storage capacity alone does not make evidence reusable. Our raw campaign record is over a gigabyte, held outside the repository, and its durability is my problem to fund. Pair storage allocations with curation help.
notes.notebook: The Warp Field Notebook is exploratory computational research with explicit limits. Its value here is the practice: numerical checks, failed attempts, corrections, and open questions, all kept and shown. Exploratory work can produce useful methods even when the hypothesis stays unproven.
notes.observatory: The Observatory is a demonstration under development. The goal is that a visitor can find an experiment, see each criterion's outcome, inspect the evidence, and follow a correction. A read-only exhibit is being prepared. I will not show you a live service and call it finished.
notes.fac: I also lead Florida Armored Combat, a nonprofit. Veterans, parents, blue-collar and white-collar members. We have a community and real questions about belonging, participation, and retention. We do not have a research partner. Where does a nonprofit go with good questions and no partner?
notes.assistance: Some projects need hands-on engineering to become usable: software engineering, validation, deployment, security, data stewardship. NSF TIP already exists. Define the missing service before proposing a new institution. Pilot a technical assistance network through existing structures.
notes.evidence: Everything I have said is backed by public repositories that keep their failures next to their successes. Six of them carry the strongest evidence. Open any one and check me.
notes.engage: Four ways to help: point me to an existing pathway, review one repository, connect a research partner for FAC, or help shape one of the three pilots: the portal, the assistance network, or the federated records.
notes.three: The Resource Guide asks for three changes in five years. Mine are access, capacity, and learning. A front door with a named person behind it. Funded engineering and validation so discoveries become usable. And shared records of what was tried and why it stopped.
notes.agenda: Everything I bring maps onto your agenda. Day one, the gap between eligibility and entry. Session one, a validated kernel library as a product. Session two, small staged awards judged by resolved uncertainty. Session three, community-to-research matching and a technical assistance network.
notes.sbir: The four SBIR readings disagree on how hard to push commercialization, but they agree on judging awards by what they produced. That takes records richer than pass or fail. That is my learning priority in their language.
notes.journey: On the Guide's path from discovery to impact, independents stall at two joints: getting into translation without an institution, and getting through validation without funded engineering. AI speeds the front of that path. It does not speed validation unless we fund checking.
